events.text: Both armies on the march. Buford's Union cavalry occupies Gettysburg. Heth's Confederate division marches east on Chambersburg Pike toward Gettysburg.
Buford dispatches pickets west and north of Gettysburg along all approach roads. Gamble's brigade occupies McPherson's Ridge. Devin's brigade screens north and east.
Heth's lead brigade (Archer) passes through Cashtown and continues east. Davis's brigade in column behind Archer. Pettigrew and Brockenbrough held in reserve at Cashtown.
Heth and Hill confer. Hill insists it is only Pennsylvania militia in Gettysburg. Heth asks permission to advance -- Hill gives approval. The battle that neither army planned begins.
events.narrative: Hill's casual permission to Heth to 'advance and get those shoes' set in motion a battle neither Lee nor Meade had chosen to fight here.

events.text: Buford's pickets on Knoxlyn Ridge first spot Heth's advance. Vedette Lieutenant Marcellus Jones fires the FIRST SHOT of the Battle of Gettysburg from a borrowed carbine. Jones fires at a Confederate officer at approximately 7:30am.
Heth's skirmishers engage Buford's dismounted cavalry. Pegram's Confederate artillery deploys on Herr Ridge. First artillery fire of the battle.
Calef's battery (Battery A, 2nd US Artillery) opens fire -- FIRST UNION ARTILLERY to fire at Gettysburg. Six guns engage Pegram's battalion in counterbattery duel.
Buford sends urgent dispatch to Reynolds: Confederates advancing in force, cavalry cannot hold long. Reynolds rides ahead of I Corps to assess situation personally.
Heth deploys Archer's brigade south of Chambersburg Pike and Davis's brigade north. Both advance in line of battle toward McPherson's Ridge. Gamble's dismounted troopers fall back slowly.
Reynolds arrives at Seminary Ridge, confers with Buford in the Seminary cupola. Reynolds sends courier ordering I Corps to rush forward at the double-quick. Confirms he will hold at all costs.
events.narrative: Reynolds's decision to hold at Gettysburg rather than fall back sealed the battle's location.

events.text: Wadsworth's division (I Corps lead) arrives at Seminary Ridge at the double-quick. Reynolds personally leads the Iron Brigade (Meredith) off the road and into Herbst Woods.
Iron Brigade double-quicks through fields toward Herbst Woods. Confederates recognize the black hats -- 'That's no militia -- that's the Army of the Potomac!' Archer's brigade halts momentarily.

REYNOLDS KILLED. Shot through the head by a sharpshooter (possibly a Confederate skirmisher) at the eastern edge of Herbst Woods while directing the Iron Brigade. Falls dead from his horse. Doubleday assumes corps command.

Iron Brigade crashes into Archer's Confederate brigade in Herbst Woods. Close-range fighting. Archer's right flank overlapped. Archer himself is CAPTURED -- first Confederate general taken since Lee assumed command. Private Patrick Maloney, 2nd Wisconsin, personally captured Archer.
Iron Brigade sweeps through Herbst Woods. Archer's brigade broken and fleeing west across Willoughby Run. I Corps establishes defensive line along McPherson's Ridge south of Chambersburg Pike.

North of the pike, Davis's Confederate brigade advances in three regiments. Cutler's Union brigade rushes to deploy north of Chambersburg Pike. Hall's battery (2nd Maine) unlimbers in the Railroad Cut area.
Davis's brigade overlaps Cutler's right flank. 76th NY and 56th PA take heavy fire and are forced back. 147th NY stands alone briefly. Meredith wounded -- Robinson assumes Iron Brigade command.
Davis's brigade pursues Cutler north. 2nd Mississippi and 42nd Mississippi enter the unfinished Railroad Cut west of the pike. Hall's battery forced to withdraw under Confederate pressure.
6th Wisconsin (Dawes) detached from Iron Brigade and ordered north across the pike. Joins 14th Brooklyn and 95th NY. Dawes orders charge directly at the Railroad Cut.

6th Wisconsin reaches the cut. Davis's Confederates trapped -- the cut at the middle position is 15 feet deep and impossible to climb under fire. Mass surrender. Dawes demands surrender: 'Where is the colonel of this regiment?' 232 Confederates captured.

Noon lull begins. Both sides reorganize. Confederate Heth, finding the resistance much heavier than expected, halts and waits for Rodes and Early to arrive from the north. Reynolds replacement confirmed as Doubleday.
events.narrative: The 'noon lull' lasted roughly 10:30am-1:00pm. Both sides used the pause to bring up reinforcements and reorganize.

events.text: I Corps completing deployment on McPherson's Ridge and Seminary Ridge. Robinson's division (2nd Division) arrives and takes position on Oak Ridge north of the pike. Buford's cavalry screens the flanks.

Rodes's Confederate division (Second Corps) arrives on Oak Hill north of Gettysburg. Rodes sees the Union I Corps position from Oak Hill. Recognizes he can attack the I Corps right flank. Begins deploying.
events.narrative: Rodes's arrival at Oak Hill was an accidental tactical gift -- he could see the exposed Union right flank from the hill.

events.text: Confederate artillery (Jones's and Andrews's battalions) deploys on Oak Hill. Carrington's and Carter's batteries open fire on Union I Corps from an enfilading position -- devastating flanking fire.

XI Corps (Howard) begins arriving north of Gettysburg. Howard takes overall command as senior officer. Schurz's division deploys north of town. Barlow's division pushes to Blocher's Knoll (Barlow's Knoll) against Howard's orders.

Rodes attacks. O'Neal's brigade miscarries -- O'Neal does not lead in person, keeps one regiment back without orders. Iverson's brigade advances in PERFECT ALIGNMENT without skirmishers toward Oak Ridge stone wall.

IVERSON'S PITS. Baxter's Union brigade (behind stone wall) fires simultaneous volley into Iverson's flank at close range. Approximately 500 Confederates shot down in minutes. Men fall in rows -- their graves visible as depressions today. Iverson reportedly does not lead the charge.
Daniel's Confederate brigade attacks south of Iverson toward the Railroad Cut area. Ramseur's brigade waits to exploit any opening. O'Neal's repulsed regiments reorganize.

GORDON'S FLANK ATTACK. Early's division arrives on York Road northeast of town. Gordon's brigade sweeps wide around the Union XI Corps right flank, hitting Barlow's position on Barlow's Knoll from the east. Doles's brigade simultaneously attacks north of town.

Barlow's Knoll overwhelmed. Barlow severely wounded -- left for dead on the knoll. Gordon personally brings him water, believing him dying. Wilkeson's Union battery destroyed on the knoll. Hays's and Avery's brigades advance south toward town.
XI Corps collapses. Barlow's and Schurz's divisions broken and streaming south through Gettysburg streets. Coster's brigade sent north to cover the retreat -- trapped in the brickyard disaster.
Coster's brigade caught from three sides in brickyard north of town -- 566 casualties in minutes. 134th NY, 154th NY, 27th PA, 73rd PA nearly destroyed as organized units.

I Corps right flank (Robinson) crumbling under Oak Hill artillery and Daniel's brigade pressure. Paul's brigade commander Paul blinded -- four successive commanders wounded. 16th Maine ordered to stay as sacrifice regiment covering the retreat.

Seminary Ridge fighting begins. Pender's Confederate division arrives and attacks I Corps position. Perrin's South Carolina brigade drives through the Lutheran Seminary grounds. Scales's brigade devastated -- 66% casualties.
Schimmelfennig cut off during retreat -- hides in a pigpen on Baltimore Street. Von Amsberg assumes XI Corps brigade command. I Corps remnants retreating through town.

Dilger's battery (Battery I, 1st Ohio) fights rearguard action THROUGH GETTYSBURG'S STREETS -- the only artillery to fight in the town itself. Engages Confederate infantry at close range on Stratton Street and Washington Street.
Union forces rally on Cemetery Hill. Howard had wisely positioned a reserve (von Steinwehr's division) here from the start. Hancock arrives from Meade -- takes command and organizes the defense.
events.narrative: Hancock's energy and presence stabilized the Union position when everything seemed lost.

events.text: LEE'S DISCRETIONARY ORDER TO EWELL: 'take Cemetery Hill if practicable.' Ewell looks at the hill, considers Johnson's division not yet arrived, decides it is not practicable. Does not order the attack.
events.narrative: Ewell's decision not to attack Cemetery Hill July 1 evening is one of the most debated command decisions of the war. Jackson would likely have attacked.

events.text: Johnson's Confederate division arrives on the Hanover Road. Positions east of Gettysburg. Faces Culp's Hill. Ewell places his corps in a line stretching from Culp's Hill to north of town.
XII Corps (Williams) arrives on Baltimore Pike and takes position on Culp's Hill. Greene's brigade on the right. Powers Hill reserve. XII Corps secures the Union right flank.
Meade replaces Doubleday with Newton to command I Corps. II Corps (Hancock) begins arriving and extending the Union line south on Cemetery Ridge. Birney's III Corps division arrives.

By nightfall the Union Army holds the fish-hook line: Cemetery Hill, Cemetery Ridge, Culp's Hill. Meade arrives in person at ~11pm. Holds council of war -- decides to stay and fight. Confederate army holds Seminary Ridge and the town.
events.narrative: The fish-hook defensive line the Union occupied at the end of July 1 was one of the strongest defensive positions of the war.

events.text: Both armies consolidate overnight positions. Lee reconnoiters the Union line from Seminary Ridge. Longstreet argues again for a strategic flanking movement. Lee overrules -- orders Longstreet to attack the Union left. The attack is to begin as early as possible.
events.narrative: Lee's decision to attack on July 2 rather than maneuver is the second most-debated Confederate command decision of the battle.

events.text: Sickles examines his assigned position on lower Cemetery Ridge and is dissatisfied. He believes the Peach Orchard ridge is higher ground and would be better. He begins to consider an unauthorized advance.

Longstreet's corps begins moving south for the flanking march. The march is complicated by the need to avoid Union observation from Little Round Top. Longstreet is slow and deliberate -- the controversial delay begins.

Berdan's sharpshooters (1st US Sharpshooters) sent into Pitzer's Woods by Sickles for reconnaissance. They find Wilcox's Confederate infantry. This confirms Confederate presence on Seminary Ridge south of town.

events.place: Warfield Ridge / south of Peach Orchard
events.text: Hood's division completes the flanking march and deploys south of Gettysburg. McLaws deploys north of Hood along Warfield Ridge. Alexander positions his artillery. The assault force is in position.

Sickles advances his entire III Corps to the Peach Orchard -- without orders, without informing Meade, without permission. Creates a salient with an exposed apex at the Orchard and a dangerously thin line stretching to Devil's Den.
events.narrative: Sickles's unauthorized advance was tactically disastrous but may have drawn Confederate attention away from the Round Tops.

events.text: Meade discovers Sickles's unauthorized advance. Furious confrontation. Meade orders Sickles back -- but Confederate artillery has already opened fire and it is too late to withdraw without chaos.

LONGSTREET'S ASSAULT BEGINS. Alexander's Confederate artillery opens fire on the Peach Orchard salient -- 54 guns. Hood's division steps off in Line of Battle heading northeast toward Devil's Den and the Round Tops.
Hood severely wounded -- arm permanently paralyzed by artillery fragment. Law assumes division command. Hood's request to swing around Big Round Top is denied by Longstreet.

events.place: Devil's Den / Little Round Top south slope
events.text: Law's brigade (formerly Hood's) reaches Big Round Top. 15th Alabama turns left and begins assaulting the southern slope of Little Round Top. Robertson's Texas Brigade engages Ward's Union brigade at Devil's Den and the Triangular Field.
Little Round Top is UNOCCUPIED by Union infantry -- only a signal station on the summit. Warren, Meade's chief engineer, realizes the danger and desperately searches for troops to send there.
events.narrative: Warren's recognition of the Little Round Top crisis and his desperate improvisation to fill it was one of the most consequential individual decisions of the battle.

events.text: Warren intercepts Vincent's brigade (V Corps) on the march and diverts it to Little Round Top without waiting for formal orders. Vincent personally leads the brigade up the hill.

Vincent's brigade arrives on Little Round Top just ahead of Law's Confederates. Vincent places his regiments on the rocky slope: 16th Michigan right, 44th NY center, 83rd PA center-left, 20th Maine on the extreme left.
15th Alabama (Oates) makes its first assault on 20th Maine's refused left flank. Chamberlain's line bends but holds. Multiple Confederate assaults follow over the next 30-40 minutes.

Vincent mortally wounded on Little Round Top. Rice assumes brigade command. Weed's brigade arrives on the summit. Hazlett drags guns up the steep rocky slope. O'Rorke's 140th NY arrives at the summit.
O'Rorke charges downhill without waiting for orders -- 140th NY sweeps Confederates off the northern slope of Little Round Top. O'Rorke shot through the neck and killed instantly.
Weed killed on the summit. Hazlett shot kneeling beside the dying Weed. Both general and artillery commander die almost simultaneously. Rittenhouse assumes battery command.
16th Michigan on Vincent's right begins to waver -- brief near-break. The regiment steadies before the line collapses. Critical moment.

CHAMBERLAIN'S BAYONET CHARGE. 20th Maine has expended nearly all ammunition after repulsing multiple assaults. Chamberlain orders a bayonet charge -- right-wheel motion sweeping down the hill. 15th Alabama broken and retreating. Nearly 400 Confederate prisoners.
McLaws's assault begins. Barksdale's Mississippi brigade charges the Peach Orchard in one of the most dramatic charges of the battle. Barksdale rides ahead of his men on horseback.
Peach Orchard salient collapses. Graham wounded and captured. 141st PA suffers 71% casualties at the apex. III Corps line crumbling from the south toward Cemetery Ridge.
Kershaw's South Carolina brigade engages in Rose Woods and the Wheatfield. DeTrobriand's Union brigade holds initially. G.T. Anderson's Georgia brigade pressing from the south.
Caldwell's II Corps division rushed south to reinforce the collapsing III Corps. Four brigades -- Cross, Kelly (Irish Brigade), Zook, Brooke -- advance into the Wheatfield.
events.narrative: Father Corby administers general absolution to the Irish Brigade before the charge. A kneeling army watches from Cemetery Ridge.

events.text: Father Corby's absolution. The Irish Brigade kneels in the field to receive general absolution before charging into the Wheatfield. One of the most dramatic religious moments of the war.
events.narrative: Corby stood on a rock and gave absolution -- all nearby troops of any faith knelt or bowed their heads.

events.text: Cross killed entering the Wheatfield. Zook mortally wounded. Brooke's brigade pushes farthest into the Wheatfield of any Union brigade. Semmes's Confederates mortally wounded.

Wofford's fresh Georgia brigade sweeps through the Wheatfield behind the retreating Caldwell -- reaches the farthest Confederate penetration toward Cemetery Ridge. Tilton's controversial withdrawal exposed the Union flank.

events.place: Wheatfield / Little Round Top west slope
events.text: Crawford's Pennsylvania Reserves charge down the western slope of Little Round Top -- drives Wofford's exhausted Confederates back through the Wheatfield. Colonel Taylor of 13th PA Reserves killed. Caldwell's position partially restored.

SICKLES WOUNDED. Artillery shell shatters Sickles's right leg near the Trostle Farm. Sickles famously smokes a cigar as he is carried from the field. Birney assumes III Corps command. Commander succession US-017 activates.

McGilvery's emergency artillery line. McGilvery assembles guns from multiple batteries -- Bigelow, Phillips, Hart -- along Plum Run to plug the gap left by III Corps collapse. Bigelow's battery ordered to hold without support.

BIGELOW'S TROSTLE FARM WITHDRAWAL. Bigelow's 9th Massachusetts battery ordered to hold as long as possible to buy time for McGilvery. Battery fights by prolonge (rope), losing guns one by one. Heroic withdrawal saves McGilvery's line.

1ST MINNESOTA'S CHARGE. Cemetery Ridge gap is open. Wilcox's Confederate brigade advancing toward the gap. Hancock has nothing to send but Colvill's 262-man 1st Minnesota. 'My God, are these all the men we have?' Orders them to charge Wilcox's entire brigade to buy 5 minutes.

1st Minnesota engages Wilcox's Confederate brigade. Both flanks overlapped but the charge stops Wilcox long enough for reinforcements to arrive. Colvill wounded, Messick killed, Coates assumes command. 85.5% casualties.
Wilcox's advance halted. Reinforcements close the gap on Cemetery Ridge. Wright's Georgia brigade briefly breaks through Cemetery Ridge north of Wilcox but is driven back without support.

Stuart arrives with his cavalry after controversial absence. Lee reportedly greets him: 'General Stuart, where have you been?' Confederate cavalry now available for the first time since before the campaign began. Commander succession CS-016 activates.

Johnson's Confederate division advances on Culp's Hill at dusk. XII Corps has been stripped away to reinforce Cemetery Ridge leaving only Greene's brigade (1,424 men) to hold the entire hill against 6,500 Confederates.
events.narrative: Greene's lone stand is one of the finest defensive performances of the war -- 1,424 men holding against 6,500.

events.text: GREENE'S LONE STAND. Greene's brigade holds Culp's Hill alone. Johnson's Confederates (Stonewall Brigade, Jones, Nicholls, Steuart) assault repeatedly. Greene extends his thin line and bends but never breaks.

Steuart's Confederate brigade occupies vacant XII Corps breastworks on lower Culp's Hill -- the right of the Union position. XII Corps (returning from Cemetery Ridge) finds their own works occupied by Confederates.
XII Corps returns to Culp's Hill and finds Confederate troops in their works. Night attack repossesses most of the upper works. Lower works remain Confederate. Sets up the July 3 morning fight.
CEMETERY HILL ASSAULT. Hays's Louisiana Tigers and Avery's North Carolina brigade charge Cemetery Hill at dusk. They reach the crest and briefly seize Union guns.

Avery mortally wounded on the slope of Cemetery Hill writing his blood message: 'Tell my father I died with my face to the enemy.' Godwin assumes brigade command. Commander succession CS-014 activates.

Carroll's Union brigade counterattacks Cemetery Hill -- drives Louisiana Tigers and Avery's brigade back down the slope. Cemetery Hill secure. The last Confederate attempt to take the Union center ends.

Willard's brigade (II Corps -- 'Harper's Ferry Cowards' seeking redemption) charges Barksdale's exhausted Confederates near Plum Run. Willard killed by artillery shell. Barksdale mortally wounded nearby. Both commanders fall almost simultaneously.

Fighting dies down across the battlefield. Both sides hold approximately their morning positions except: Confederates hold lower Culp's Hill works. Union line on Cemetery Ridge is intact. III Corps is shattered. The enormous cost of July 2 becomes clear.
events.narrative: July 2 was the bloodiest single day of the Gettysburg campaign -- approximately 20,000 total casualties across both armies.

events.text: Lee and Longstreet meet. Lee decides to attack Cemetery Ridge with Pickett's fresh division plus Pettigrew and Trimble July 3. Longstreet argues against it: 'General, I have been a soldier all my life... it is my opinion that no 15,000 men ever arrayed for battle can take that position.' Lee overrules.
events.narrative: This exchange -- Longstreet's most famous protest -- became the center of the Lost Cause argument that Longstreet lost Gettysburg. Most historians side with Longstreet's assessment.

events.text: Alexander begins positioning Confederate artillery along Seminary Ridge for the July 3 cannonade. Approximately 170 guns will fire tomorrow. The ammunition situation is already tight.
Meade holds council of war. All corps commanders polled -- decision is unanimous to remain and fight on July 3. Meade predicts Lee will attack his center. He is correct.
events.narrative: Meade's prediction that Lee would attack his center on July 3 is one of the most accurate command predictions of the war.

events.text: Both armies settle in for the night. Pickett's division -- fresh, not yet engaged -- moves into position behind Seminary Ridge. Pettigrew's and Trimble's commands positioned on Seminary Ridge left.
Johnson's Confederates dig in on lower Culp's Hill. XII Corps prepares for the morning counterattack. Meade orders artillery chief Hunt to conserve ammunition -- critical decision for July 3.

End of Day 2. Tallying casualties: approximately 10,000 Union, 10,000 Confederate. III Corps effectively destroyed as a fighting force. Both Round Tops firmly in Union hands. Cemetery Hill and Culp's Hill (mostly) held. Lee will attack the center tomorrow.

Day 3 opens with Union XII Corps artillery firing on Johnson's Confederates dug into the lower Culp's Hill breastworks. The bombardment opens the longest sustained infantry fight of the battle -- seven hours.

Johnson's Confederate division counterattacks to retain the breastworks. Stonewall Brigade, Jones, Nicholls, Steuart assault the XII Corps line. Greene's brigade and returning XII Corps units resist along the hillside works.

Steuart's Confederate brigade makes repeated assaults up the steep hill. 1st Maryland Confederate and 3rd NC suffer heavy casualties. The parallel fight between Union and Confederate Maryland regiments is ongoing here.

Colgrove's controversial charge. Mudge's 2nd Massachusetts and 27th Indiana ordered to charge across an open meadow toward Confederate positions. Mudge's last words: 'It is murder but it is the order.' Mudge killed leading the charge.
Both sides fight a grinding attritional battle on Culp's Hill. Johnson's Confederates make twelve distinct assaults. XII Corps holds the upper works throughout. Confederate ammunition running low.
XII Corps counterattacks aggressively. Candy's, Kane's, and Greene's brigades advance to recapture lower works. Johnson's division slowly pushed back. Steuart's brigade suffering severely.
Johnson's Confederate assault on Culp's Hill exhausted. Confederate ammunition nearly expended. Johnson signals Ewell that he cannot continue. Ewell orders Johnson to hold what he has.

Pickett's fresh division moves up behind Seminary Ridge in preparation for the afternoon assault. The three Virginia brigades (Garnett, Kemper, Armistead) form in the woods, invisible to Union observers.

Pettigrew's division (Heth's old command) and Trimble's two brigades (Lane and Scales/Lowrance) positioned on Seminary Ridge left of Pickett. The assault force numbers approximately 12,500 men across a mile front.
Final Culp's Hill fighting. XII Corps retakes most of the contested works. Johnson's remaining Confederates hold a small section of the lower works but are effectively contained.

Culp's Hill fighting finally ends at approximately 11:00am. Johnson's division retires. Twelve Confederate assaults repulsed. Union line on Culp's Hill completely restored. Total Culp's Hill casualties: approximately 3,500 across both days.
events.narrative: The seven-hour Culp's Hill fight was the longest sustained infantry battle of Gettysburg but is overshadowed by Pickett's Charge in popular memory.

events.text: Alexander positions the Confederate artillery along Seminary Ridge for the cannonade. 170 Confederate guns arranged in a two-mile arc from the Peach Orchard north to the Hagerstown Road. Alexander writes two famous messages to Pickett.

THE CANNONADE BEGINS. At approximately 1:00pm, two Confederate signal guns fire in sequence. 170 Confederate guns open fire simultaneously -- the largest artillery bombardment in the history of the Western Hemisphere to that date. The sound is heard in Philadelphia, 140 miles away.
events.narrative: Alexander later wrote that the cannonade was the most magnificent spectacle he ever witnessed. The Union artillery chief Hunt deliberately slowed Union counter-fire to conserve ammunition.

events.text: Hunt deliberately silences Union artillery to conserve ammunition for the infantry assault. Hancock overrules Hunt and orders the guns to keep firing for morale. The disagreement between Hunt and Hancock shapes the eventual repulse.
events.narrative: Hunt's decision to conserve ammunition was tactically correct. Hancock's decision to keep firing boosted infantry morale but depleted artillery reserves.

events.text: Confederate artillery fire overshooting Cemetery Ridge -- most shells landing behind the Union line near Taneytown Road. Union artillery casualties lighter than expected. Meade's headquarters nearly hit.
events.narrative: The Confederate tendency to overshoot was a significant tactical failure -- the cannonade inflicted far less damage on the Union infantry than Lee and Alexander had hoped.

events.text: Alexander's first message to Pickett: 'For God's sake come quick or we cannot support you -- ammunition nearly exhausted.' Pickett shows it to Longstreet. Longstreet cannot speak -- nods his head. The charge is set in motion.
events.narrative: Longstreet later wrote: 'I could not speak. I bowed in answer.' His reluctance to order the charge is evident in every account.

events.text: Alexander's second message to Pickett: 'I would not make the charge now -- but the order has been given and the troops are already moving.' Pickett's division steps out of the woods.

Union artillery falls silent -- Confederate infantry interpret this as success of the cannonade. In fact Hunt has ordered silence to conserve ammunition. Confederate infantry begin dressing their lines in the open.
Stannard's Vermont Brigade (I Corps) takes position south of The Angle on Cemetery Ridge. Stannard has a clear view of Kemper's right flank. He is already planning the flanking maneuver.

PICKETT'S CHARGE BEGINS. The entire Confederate assault force -- approximately 12,500 men in a mile-wide front -- steps off Seminary Ridge in Line of Battle heading east across the open fields toward Cemetery Ridge. The most famous infantry assault in American history.
Union artillery opens with solid shot then shell as the Confederate line advances across the open ground. Each discharge tears gaps in the Confederate line. The attackers close ranks and keep moving.

BROCKENBROUGH COLLAPSES. The far Confederate left (Brockenbrough's Virginia brigade) breaks and retreats under flanking fire from the 8th Ohio's advanced skirmish position. Pettigrew's left flank is now exposed.

Confederate assault line reaches the Emmitsburg Road and crosses the fencing. Heavy casualties from Union artillery and musketry. Kemper's brigade begins obliquing left toward the Copse of Trees -- exposing its right flank.

STANNARD'S FLANKING ATTACK. Stannard's Vermont brigade wheels left 90 degrees and pours enfilade fire into Kemper's exposed right flank. The 13th and 14th Vermont fire into the Confederate right. Kemper's brigade takes devastating flank fire.
Kemper severely wounded in the Confederate assault. Mayo assumes brigade command. Kemper briefly captured, then rescued by his men. Commander succession CS-006 activates.

Pettigrew's Confederate brigades (26th NC, 11th NC, 47th NC, 52nd NC) reach the stone wall on Cemetery Ridge north of The Angle. Union II Corps (Smyth, Hays) fires at close range. 12th NJ fires buck-and-ball at point-blank range.

Garnett's Confederate brigade reaches the stone wall at The Angle. Heavy casualties from canister. Garnett rides on horseback (too ill to walk) -- conspicuous and exposed. The two lines exchange fire at close range across the wall.

GARNETT KIA. Shot from his horse at The Angle -- his body never officially identified after the battle. Marshall killed leading Pettigrew's brigade. Multiple Confederate commanders fall almost simultaneously.

ARMISTEAD LEADS MEN OVER THE WALL. Armistead places his hat on his sword as a guide and leads his brigade over the stone wall at The Angle -- the deepest Confederate penetration of the battle. Approximately 150-200 men cross with him.

ARMISTEAD MORTALLY WOUNDED. Shot moments after crossing the wall -- while touching a Union gun with his hand. Falls beyond the stone wall among Union troops. Armistead asks for Hancock to be brought to him. Hancock also wounded at this moment.

CUSHING KIA. Lieutenant Cushing, serving his last two guns at The Angle, shot through the mouth and killed. Sergeant Fuger assumes command of the shattered battery. Commander succession US-023 activates.

Cowan's Union battery fires canister into Armistead's men at approximately 50 yards -- devastating close-range fire. Union infantry closes from multiple directions. The Confederate penetration is contained and then driven back.
The Confederate penetration is broken. Armistead's men streaming back over the wall or surrendering. Devereux's 19th Massachusetts and others pour into the breach. The Angle is secured.

Along the entire line the Confederate assault collapses. Pettigrew's brigades fall back. Trimble (wounded) orders retreat. The survivors stream back toward Seminary Ridge. Lee rides forward to meet them: 'It is all my fault.'
events.narrative: Lee's acknowledgment -- 'It is all my fault' -- is one of the most famous statements of the war. He met his broken men personally and attempted to rally them for a Union counterattack that never came.

events.text: 16TH VERMONT SECOND WHEEL. Stannard's 16th VT wheels again -- now against Wilcox's and Lang's Confederate brigades advancing in belated support of Pickett. The double enfilade effectively seals the repulse on the south end.

events.place: East Cavalry Field (3 miles east of Gettysburg)
events.text: EAST CAVALRY FIELD. Stuart's cavalry (Hampton, Fitz Lee, Chambliss) attacks east of Gettysburg attempting to reach the Union rear during the main assault. Gregg and Custer's Michigan Brigade block the advance.

CUSTER'S CHARGE. Custer personally leads the Michigan Brigade in a mounted charge shouting 'Come on you Wolverines!' The charge stops Stuart's advance. Hampton wounded in melee -- sabre cut to head. Commander succession CS-017 activates.

Stuart's cavalry repulsed at East Cavalry Field. The Confederate cavalry's last chance to reach the Union rear during Pickett's Charge is gone. Pennington's Union horse artillery fires in support throughout.

KILPATRICK'S CHARGE. Kilpatrick orders Farnsworth's cavalry brigade to charge Confederate infantry south of the battlefield. Farnsworth protests: the charge is suicidal over rocky terrain against formed infantry.
FARNSWORTH KIA. Farnsworth leads the doomed charge and is killed -- a general for only four days. The charge accomplishes nothing. Kilpatrick's decision is universally condemned.
Meade considers a counterattack. Hancock (wounded) urges one. Meade decides the army is too disorganized and depleted. The counterattack that might have destroyed Lee's army does not happen.
events.narrative: Meade's failure to counterattack after Pickett's repulse is his most criticized decision of the battle.

events.text: Lee begins organizing his army for defense -- expecting Meade's counterattack. When it doesn't come, Lee begins considering withdrawal. Ewell, Hill, and Longstreet ordered to consolidate.
Both armies largely stationary. Union troops bury the dead and collect wounded. Confederate artillery conserves remaining ammunition. Lee confers with his corps commanders about the retreat.
Lee orders the retreat to begin on July 4. Imboden's cavalry will escort the enormous wagon train of wounded -- 17 miles long. Lee takes full responsibility for the defeat.
events.narrative: Imboden described Lee at this moment: 'I never saw a man so agitated in my life' -- pacing back and forth, saying over and over 'Too bad. Too bad. Oh, too bad.'

events.text: Rain begins. Both armies exhausted. The Battle of Gettysburg is effectively over. Union casualties: approximately 23,000. Confederate casualties: approximately 28,000. Total: ~51,000 in three days.

END OF THE BATTLE. Total Confederate losses approximately 37% of the army engaged. Total Union losses approximately 25%. The Confederate Army of Northern Virginia will never again mount a strategic offensive into the North. The High Water Mark of the Confederacy has passed.
events.narrative: Gettysburg, combined with Vicksburg's fall on July 4, marks the turning point of the Civil War. The Confederacy would fight on for nearly two more years but the strategic initiative passed permanently to the Union.

stories.title: The First Shot
stories.summary: At approximately 7:30am on July 1, 1863, Lieutenant Marcellus Jones of the 8th Illinois Cavalry fired the first shot of the Battle of Gettysburg. He borrowed a carbine from a sergeant, rested it on a fence rail, and fired at a distant Confederate officer. The shot missed -- but 51,000 casualties would follow.
stories.script:
The morning of July 1 was warm and hazy when Corporal Alphonso Hodges spotted movement on the Chambersburg Pike. He reported to his sergeant: Confederate infantry, coming in force.

Lieutenant Marcellus Jones, commanding the vedette post of Company E, 8th Illinois Cavalry, borrowed Sergeant Levi Shafer's carbine. He rested the barrel on a fence rail along the Knoxlyn Ridge. In the distance, perhaps 700 yards away, a mounted Confederate officer rode along the pike ahead of his advancing column.

Jones squeezed the trigger.

The shot missed. The officer rode on. But the sound of that single shot rolled across the fields and into the histories of both nations.

It was approximately 7:30 in the morning. The Battle of Gettysburg had begun.

Jones had no way of knowing what his missed shot had set in motion. He could not know that 51,000 men would become casualties on this ground over the next three days. He could not know that the shot he had just fired -- borrowed, aimed from a fence rail, and wasted -- would be commemorated by a monument that still stands on Knoxlyn Ridge today.

He rode back to report what he had seen. Behind him, Heth's Confederate division continued its march toward Gettysburg.

stories.title: Reynolds Falls
stories.place: Eastern edge of Herbst Woods, McPherson's Ridge
stories.summary: Major General John Reynolds, the finest corps commander in the Army of the Potomac, was killed at approximately 10:15am while personally leading the Iron Brigade into Herbst Woods. Shot through the head, he fell dead from his horse. He was 42 years old. His death left a void in Union command that was never truly filled.
stories.script:
John Fulton Reynolds was, by nearly universal agreement, the best corps commander in the Army of the Potomac. Meade had offered him command of the entire army three days earlier. Reynolds had refused -- he wanted the freedom to fight without political interference. He had ridden ahead of his corps to Gettysburg that morning to see the situation for himself.

What he saw at the Seminary convinced him that the Union army had to fight here. He sent a courier galloping south: bring the I Corps forward at the double-quick. And then, because Reynolds was that kind of general, he did not wait at the Seminary. He rode forward to lead the attack himself.

The Iron Brigade -- his beloved Iron Brigade -- was double-quicking across the fields toward the dark woods of Herbst. Reynolds rode to their head. He waved them forward into the trees, shouting encouragement.

The shot came without warning.

It struck Reynolds behind the right ear. He fell from his saddle without a word. By the time his aides reached him, he was already dead.

He was 42 years old. He had never married. He had been engaged to a woman named Kate Hewitt; her name was found on a ring he wore. She had been waiting for him.

The Iron Brigade went into Herbst Woods and broke Archer's Confederate brigade -- the attack Reynolds had set in motion with his life. But Reynolds was gone, and the Army of the Potomac would fight the next two days without the man who might have made all the difference.

stories.title: Archer Captured
stories.summary: Within minutes of Reynolds's death, the Iron Brigade's charge through Herbst Woods captured Confederate General James Archer -- the first Confederate general officer taken prisoner since Lee assumed command of the army. Private Patrick Maloney of the 2nd Wisconsin personally seized Archer as he tried to escape across Willoughby Run.
stories.script:
The Iron Brigade swept through Herbst Woods like a tide. Archer's Tennessee and Alabama brigade had advanced confidently that morning -- they expected Pennsylvania militia, not the best infantry in the Army of the Potomac.

The black hats changed everything. A Confederate soldier who recognized them shouted a warning: 'That's no militia -- that's the Army of the Potomac!' But it was too late.

The Iron Brigade's left regiments -- the 2nd and 7th Wisconsin -- swept south of the Chambersburg Pike and curled around Archer's right flank. Archer's brigade, caught in the flank, broke. Men streamed back toward Willoughby Run, some plunging into the water to escape.

Brigadier General James J. Archer was trying to cross the run when Private Patrick Maloney of the 2nd Wisconsin grabbed him by the collar.

Archer was a small, sick man -- he had been ill for weeks and had no business commanding a brigade in the field. He looked up at the private holding him and said simply that he would not be taken.

Maloney held on.

Archer was brought to Doubleday, who had just assumed command after Reynolds's death. The two men knew each other from before the war. Doubleday extended his hand and said cheerfully, 'Good morning, Archer! How are you? I am glad to see you!'

Archer refused to shake hands. 'Well, I am not glad to see YOU by a damn sight, Doubleday.'

He was the first Confederate general officer captured since Lee had taken command of the Army of Northern Virginia. He would spend the rest of the campaign in a Union prison.

stories.title: The Railroad Cut
stories.place: Unfinished Railroad Cut, north of Chambersburg Pike
stories.summary: Colonel Rufus Dawes led the 6th Wisconsin in a desperate charge across the Chambersburg Pike and into the unfinished Railroad Cut, where Davis's Confederate brigade had taken cover. The cut proved a trap -- too deep to escape under fire. The 6th Wisconsin captured 232 men in one of the most decisive small-unit actions of the battle.
stories.script:
Rufus Dawes had been a schoolteacher before the war. On the morning of July 1, 1863, he was commanding the 6th Wisconsin -- the largest regiment in the Iron Brigade -- and watching Davis's Confederate brigade sweep north past his position toward the unfinished railroad cut.

Dawes received orders to charge. He turned to his men.

'Six Wisconsin, advance!' The regiment stepped off at the double-quick, moving north across the Chambersburg Pike. The 14th Brooklyn -- red-legged Zouaves -- joined on their left. The 95th New York came with them.

Davis's men had ducked into the railroad cut for cover. It seemed perfect -- a ready-made trench running east-west. What Davis had not understood was that the western portion of the cut was fifteen feet deep. His men were trapped in a ditch.

Dawes's regiment hit the cut at a run. The fighting was vicious -- men stabbed each other with bayonets across a gap of feet, grappled over regimental flags, fired at point-blank range. But the Confederates could not climb the sheer walls under fire.

Dawes reached the middle of the cut and shouted across to the Confederate officer opposite him: 'Where is the colonel of this regiment?'

'Who are you?' the officer called back.

'I am Colonel Dawes of the 6th Wisconsin. I demand the immediate and unconditional surrender of this regiment!'

There was a pause. Then the Confederate flag dipped, and men began throwing down their arms.

Dawes captured 232 prisoners -- nearly a full regiment -- in a single charge. The regimental flag of the 2nd Mississippi was taken. Davis's brigade had been broken for the second time in a morning.

stories.title: Iverson's Pits
stories.place: Oak Ridge stone wall, north of Gettysburg
stories.summary: Brigadier General Alfred Iverson sent his North Carolina brigade forward without skirmishers, without reconnaissance, and apparently without personally leading the charge. His men advanced in perfect alignment directly toward a stone wall behind which Baxter's Union brigade lay waiting. In minutes, approximately 500 of Iverson's 1,470 men were shot down in rows. The shallow graves of his men are visible as depressions in the ground at Oak Ridge to this day.
stories.script:
The field north of Gettysburg was quiet when Iverson's four North Carolina regiments stepped off. They moved in perfect alignment -- a textbook advance that would have drawn admiration on a parade ground. No skirmishers preceded them. No one had scouted the stone wall ahead.

Behind that wall, Baxter's Union brigade lay flat in the grass, waiting. The 12th Massachusetts, 83rd New York, 97th New York, 88th Pennsylvania, 90th Pennsylvania -- all pressed close to the ground, rifles ready.

Iverson's men had covered perhaps half the distance when Baxter's soldiers rose up behind the wall and fired.

The volley came simultaneously along a front of several hundred yards. Iverson's regiments were struck in the flank -- the wall ran parallel to their line of advance. Men fell in rows exactly as they had been marching, in perfect military alignment, because there had been no time to break formation before the fire swept through them.

About 500 men fell in the first minutes. Not wounded -- fell, shot, lying in the grass in the same lines they had been marching in.

Iverson, watching from behind, reportedly believed his men had surrendered. He sent word to Rodes that his brigade had thrown up the white flag in dishonor. It was not true. His men were not surrendering. They were dying.

When Union soldiers advanced after the battle to bury the dead, they found the bodies lying in such perfect order that little digging was needed. They buried them where they fell, in shallow trenches that followed the line of the advance.

The slight depressions of those graves are visible at Oak Ridge today.

Iverson was relieved of command shortly after the battle. He was never given another brigade.

stories.title: Gordon and Barlow
stories.summary: When Gordon's Confederate brigade swept over Barlow's Knoll, General Francis Barlow was shot and left for dead among his fallen men. Confederate General John Gordon rode to the dying Union general, gave him water, tried to comfort him, and promised to find his wife. The two men met again after the war and became friends -- one of the most remarkable reconciliation stories of the conflict.
stories.script:
The charge of Gordon's Georgia brigade had swept everything before it. When it was over, when the Union line on Barlow's Knoll had collapsed and the Confederates were pursuing the broken XI Corps south toward Gettysburg, John Gordon rode over the ground his men had taken.

He found a Union general lying among the dead, shot through the body and left behind in the rout. The man was barely conscious.

Gordon dismounted. He raised the officer's head, gave him water from his own canteen, tried to make him comfortable. He asked if there was anything he could do.

The dying man -- it was General Francis Barlow, commanding the First Division of the XI Corps -- said he did not expect to live. He asked Gordon, if it were possible, to find his wife and tell her where he had fallen.

Gordon promised. He had the general moved to a shaded spot and left a Confederate soldier to care for him. Then he rejoined the pursuit.

Barlow did not die. Against all expectation, he recovered -- slowly, painfully -- and returned to command. He served through the rest of the war. He became one of the best Union division commanders at the Overland Campaign.

After the war, Gordon heard a rumor that Barlow had died. Barlow heard a rumor that Gordon had died. They never sought each other out.

Years later, at a dinner party in Washington, two men were introduced and recognized each other simultaneously.

It was Gordon. It was Barlow.

They had both assumed the other was dead. They became friends. Gordon told the story many times in his postwar lectures -- the enemy officer he had cared for on the field at Gettysburg, the man he had thought was dying, sitting across a dinner table from him in the nation's capital.

'We became fast friends,' Gordon wrote, 'and so we shall remain while we both live.'

stories.title: Berdan's Reconnaissance
stories.summary: Colonel Hiram Berdan led his regiment of green-uniformed sharpshooters into Pitzer's Woods on a reconnaissance ordered by Sickles. They found Wilcox's Confederate infantry already positioned there -- confirming Confederate activity on Seminary Ridge south of town. The reconnaissance gave Sickles his justification for advancing to the Peach Orchard.
stories.script:
The sharpshooters of Berdan's regiment were the best shots in the Union Army. Recruited for their marksmanship, equipped with Sharps repeating rifles, dressed in green uniforms that made them harder to see in the woods -- they were an elite within an army that still largely fought in shoulder-to-shoulder lines.

On the morning of July 2, Sickles was worried about his left. Buford's cavalry had departed. There was open ground stretching south and west, and nobody knew what was on the other side of Pitzer's Woods on Seminary Ridge.

Sickles ordered Berdan to find out.

The 1st US Sharpshooters moved into the woods in skirmish order -- open files, each man moving independently, using cover. No solid lines. No drumbeats. Just green-coated men filtering into the dark trees.

They found Wilcox's Alabama brigade.

The firefight was sharp and brief. The sharpshooters fell back with their information: there were Confederate infantry on Seminary Ridge, south of town, already in position. Longstreet's corps was there.

Berdan returned with his report. Sickles had what he needed.

Whether the reconnaissance actually showed what Sickles claimed it showed -- a Confederate flanking movement about to swing around his left -- is a matter historians still debate. What is certain is that Sickles used it as justification for advancing his entire corps to the Emmitsburg Road without orders. Whether Berdan's intelligence warranted that response, and whether the advance saved or nearly destroyed the Army of the Potomac, has been argued for 160 years.

stories.title: Sickles Moves Forward
stories.summary: Against direct orders, General Daniel Sickles advanced his entire III Corps nearly a mile forward from its assigned position on Cemetery Ridge to the Peach Orchard on the Emmitsburg Road. The move created a dangerously exposed salient. When Longstreet's assault struck it that afternoon, the salient collapsed in catastrophe -- but Sickles would spend the rest of his long life arguing he had been right.
stories.script:
Daniel Sickles was a politician, a killer, and -- in his own estimation -- a military genius. He had shot his wife's lover on the steps of the White House and been acquitted by reason of temporary insanity -- the first successful use of that defense in American legal history. He had wangled a general's commission despite no military training whatsoever. He had survived every disaster through audacity, charm, and a complete inability to recognize that he might be wrong.

On the morning of July 2, 1863, he stared at the ground his corps had been assigned and decided it was unsuitable. The Peach Orchard, a quarter-mile to the west along the Emmitsburg Road, sat on slightly higher ground. In Sickles's judgment, the Peach Orchard was the position he should hold.

He did not ask Meade. He did not request permission. He did not inform his commander.

Around 3:00 in the afternoon, Sickles moved his entire corps -- 10,000 men and dozens of artillery pieces -- forward to the Emmitsburg Road.

Meade discovered the movement and rode south in fury. He found Sickles sitting on horseback in the new line and demanded an explanation. Sickles began to explain. Meade interrupted: the position was untenable. The line was too long. The flanks were exposed. The corps should go back.

At that moment, Longstreet's guns opened fire.

'I will withdraw if you order it,' Sickles said.

'I do order it,' Meade replied. 'But the enemy will not allow you to.'

He was right. Within the hour, the Peach Orchard would become the most violent piece of ground on the continent.

Sickles lost his right leg to an artillery shell that afternoon. He was carried from the field smoking a cigar -- a gesture for his men. He spent the rest of his life, another fifty years, insisting that his unauthorized advance had saved the Army of the Potomac by drawing Confederate attention away from Little Round Top. Most historians disagree. But Sickles never changed his story.

stories.title: Vincent and Little Round Top
stories.summary: With Little Round Top undefended and Confederate infantry racing to take it, General Warren intercepted Vincent's brigade on the march and redirected it up the hill. Vincent placed his regiments on the slope just minutes before Law's Confederates arrived. Colonel Strong Vincent was mortally wounded holding the position he had seized -- he died a brigadier general, his promotion arriving while he lay dying.
stories.script:
Gouverneur Warren stood on the summit of Little Round Top and understood in an instant what was about to happen.

The hill was empty. Below and to the south, through his field glasses, he could see the glint of sunlight on rifle barrels and bayonets -- Law's Confederate division moving through the trees at the base of Big Round Top, angling toward the rocky slope where Warren stood alone.

If the Confederates took Little Round Top, their artillery would command the entire Union line on Cemetery Ridge from the south. The army would have to retreat or be destroyed. Warren sent aides galloping in every direction: get troops, any troops, get them up this hill now.

The first aide found Colonel Strong Vincent commanding his brigade on the road below. Vincent did not wait for formal orders -- he did not have time for formal orders. 'I will take the responsibility of taking my brigade there,' he told the aide, and immediately led his four regiments up the rocky face of Little Round Top.

Vincent placed his regiments himself, walking the ground with quick precision: 16th Michigan on the right, 44th New York in the center, 83rd Pennsylvania center-left, 20th Maine on the extreme left. He was explicit about the left: 'This is the left of the Union line. You must hold this ground at all costs.'

He said this to Colonel Joshua Chamberlain of the 20th Maine.

Within minutes of the last regiment reaching its position, Confederate infantry appeared at the base of the slope.

Vincent was shot through the groin late in the afternoon while trying to rally the 16th Michigan. His men carried him from the field. He lingered for five days. On July 7, as he was dying, word came that he had been promoted to brigadier general. Those around him told him the news. He smiled.

'Did I not tell you that I would be a general officer before the battle was over?' he said.

He died that afternoon.

stories.title: Chamberlain's Charge
stories.summary: After repulsing five Confederate assaults with nearly empty cartridge boxes, Colonel Joshua Chamberlain ordered the 20th Maine to fix bayonets and charge downhill. The attack swept the 15th Alabama from the slope and captured nearly 400 prisoners. It was the most celebrated regimental action of the battle -- and possibly of the entire war.
stories.script:
Joshua Chamberlain had been a professor of rhetoric at Bowdoin College before the war. He had taught himself tactics by reading military manuals at night. On the afternoon of July 2, 1863, he had already repulsed five Confederate assaults on the left flank of the entire Union Army.

His regiment was nearly out of ammunition.

The 15th Alabama, under Colonel William Oates, had been trying to turn the 20th Maine's refused left flank for nearly an hour. Each time, Chamberlain's men had stopped them. But the cartridge boxes were almost empty. The men were telling their officers they had nothing left to fire.

Oates was preparing another charge.

Chamberlain had two choices: retreat, or attack. Retreat was unacceptable -- his orders were to hold at all costs. Attack with empty rifles seemed suicidal. But Chamberlain understood something Oates did not: the Confederates below were as exhausted as the men above. The 15th Alabama had marched twenty-five miles that day before climbing and assaulting the hill. If he could shock them with an unexpected counter-charge, they might break before they understood what was happening.

'Fix bayonets,' Chamberlain ordered.

The command passed down the line. The 20th Maine -- fewer than 200 men still standing in the ranks -- fixed bayonets.

'Charge!'

The regiment swept downhill in a right-wheel motion, pivoting around the center and sweeping south and west. Chamberlain led from the front, a pistol in one hand and a saber in the other.

Oates's men, climbing uphill toward what they expected to be a final assault on a shattered regiment, were instead hit by a wall of screaming men coming downhill at them.

The 15th Alabama broke.

The 20th Maine captured nearly 400 prisoners. Chamberlain was slightly wounded -- twice. He would receive the Medal of Honor for his actions on Little Round Top, presented thirty years after the battle. At the war's end, Ulysses Grant chose Chamberlain to receive the formal Confederate surrender at Appomattox.

stories.title: Bigelow's Last Stand
stories.summary: Captain John Bigelow's 9th Massachusetts Battery was ordered to hold the Trostle Farm without infantry support -- to buy time for McGilvery to form the artillery line that would stop the Confederate breakthrough. The battery fought its withdrawal by prolonge, losing men and guns but accomplishing its mission. A cannonball through the barn wall is still visible today.
stories.script:
Lieutenant Colonel McGilvery rode up to Captain John Bigelow at a gallop.

'I must have time,' McGilvery said. 'You must stay here and hold at any cost until I can form a new line.'

Bigelow looked around. His battery -- six Napoleon guns, nine horses each -- was already under fire from Barksdale's Mississippi infantry advancing from the Peach Orchard. There was no infantry support anywhere nearby. McGilvery was asking him to hold a position unsupported against a brigade of Confederate infantry.

'How long?' Bigelow asked.

'As long as you can,' McGilvery said, and rode away.

Bigelow ordered his battery to hook their guns to prolonges -- long ropes that allowed artillerymen to move the guns while still firing -- and begin a fighting withdrawal through the Trostle Farm lane.

What followed was one of the most desperate artillery actions of the war. The 9th Massachusetts fired as they retreated, horses falling, men dropping at the guns. Bigelow was wounded. The battery lost one gun stuck in a stone wall as Confederate infantry closed in from three sides. The last section fired canister into advancing Mississippians from a range of fifty yards.

Bigelow lost 28 men and one gun. He bought McGilvery the twenty minutes he needed.

When Confederate infantry finally overran the Trostle Farm, they found it abandoned. McGilvery's Plum Run Line was formed and waiting.

The cannonball hole in the Trostle Farm barn wall -- a Confederate artillery round that missed Bigelow's withdrawing battery -- is still visible today. It is one of the most photographed details on the Gettysburg battlefield.

stories.title: The First Minnesota
stories.place: Cemetery Ridge south, near Plum Run
stories.summary: With Cemetery Ridge open and Wilcox's Confederate brigade advancing toward the gap, General Hancock turned to the only regiment near at hand -- 262 men of the 1st Minnesota. He ordered them to charge an entire Confederate brigade to buy five minutes for reinforcements to arrive. They did it. 224 of 262 men fell. The regiment suffered the highest casualty rate of any Union regiment in a single engagement in the entire war.
stories.script:
Winfield Scott Hancock had been riding hard along Cemetery Ridge for twenty minutes, trying to hold together a line that was dissolving in front of him. The III Corps was gone -- shattered, streaming back from the Peach Orchard and the Wheatfield. The gap in the Union center was real and it was widening.

Across the fields, Cadmus Wilcox's Alabama brigade was advancing at the double-quick toward that gap. If they reached Cemetery Ridge, the Union line would be cut in two.

Hancock turned in his saddle. The only regiment near at hand was the 1st Minnesota -- 262 officers and men under Colonel William Colvill.

'My God, are these all the men we have here?' Hancock said.

Then he ordered them forward.

Colvill understood what the order meant. He turned to his regiment: 'Forward, double-quick!'

The 262 men of the 1st Minnesota -- a state with fewer than 200,000 people -- charged into Wilcox's entire brigade.

The fighting was savage and brief. The regiment drove into the Confederate line with bayonets and clubbed rifles, and for a few minutes the Confederate advance actually stopped. The Alabamians had not expected this. They had not expected anything to be there at all.

But 262 men cannot hold long against 1,700. The 1st Minnesota was shredded. Colvill went down, shot in three places. The regimental commander, the lieutenant colonel, the major -- all hit. Companies were reduced to handfuls. The regiment fell back toward Cemetery Ridge.

But they had bought the five minutes Hancock needed. Reinforcements arrived and closed the gap.

Of 262 men who charged, 224 were casualties -- 85.5%. It remains the highest casualty rate suffered by any Union regiment in a single engagement in the entire war.

The survivors -- 38 men -- formed in line the next morning and were ordered to hold the same ground. They did.

stories.title: Greene's Lone Stand
stories.summary: When the XII Corps was stripped from Culp's Hill to reinforce Cemetery Ridge, only George Greene's New York brigade remained -- 1,424 men to hold the position against Johnson's entire Confederate division of 6,500. Greene extended his line impossibly thin and held for three hours. It was one of the finest defensive performances of the entire war.
stories.script:
The orders came at dusk: Slocum was pulling the XII Corps south to reinforce the crumbling Union left. The brigades would move -- all of them. All except Greene's.

Brigadier General George Greene was sixty-two years old, the oldest brigade commander at Gettysburg. He was a West Point engineer who had spent his career building aqueducts and railroads. His five New York regiments -- 1,424 men -- were to hold Culp's Hill while the rest of the corps departed.

Greene looked at his line. His five regiments normally occupied perhaps 600 yards of front. The entire XII Corps position was more than 1,300 yards. He was being asked to hold more than double his normal front -- with the same number of men -- against Johnson's Confederate division of 6,500.

Greene had spent his career as an engineer. He understood defensive works. During the afternoon, while the army was fighting in the south, he had ordered his men to build breastworks -- proper log-and-earth fortifications, not just scratched rifle pits. His officers had thought it excessive. Now those breastworks would save his command.

Greene extended his line by thinning it beyond any conventional military standard. A man here, a man there, a twenty-foot gap between. The works did the work that bodies could not.

Johnson's division attacked in waves. The Stonewall Brigade, Jones's brigade, Nicholls's brigade -- all came up the dark hill into the abatis and the fire from Greene's thin line.

Greene held.

For three hours, 1,424 men held Culp's Hill against 6,500. Steuart's brigade, on the Confederate left, found the empty XII Corps works and occupied them -- but they could not advance past Greene's position. The upper hill stayed Union.

When the XII Corps returned in the darkness, they found Greene still holding, his line still unbroken. He had lost 303 men. He had saved the Union right flank.

stories.title: The Louisiana Tigers on Cemetery Hill
stories.summary: At dusk on July 2, Hays's Louisiana Tigers and Avery's North Carolina brigade stormed Cemetery Hill in near-darkness. They reached the crest, seized Union artillery, and held it briefly -- the closest any Confederate force came to breaking the Union center. Colonel Avery was mortally wounded on the slope, writing his last message in his own blood.
stories.script:
The Louisiana Tigers had a reputation. In an army of hard men they were considered especially dangerous -- New Orleans toughs, dock workers, immigrants, men with nothing to lose. Their officers sometimes controlled them with threats of summary execution. On the battlefield, they were formidable.

At dusk on July 2, Hays's five Louisiana regiments and Avery's three North Carolina regiments stepped off from the town of Gettysburg and began climbing Cemetery Hill.

The timing was not accidental. The Union artillery on the hill could not depress their guns enough to fire directly at men climbing the steep slope below them. The light was failing. The Confederate attack would have to be met with musketry alone.

Hays's men swept up the hill with a ferocity that overwhelmed the XI Corps units defending the lower slope. They reached the crest. They seized the Union guns. For a few minutes -- perhaps ten, perhaps fifteen -- Louisiana and North Carolina men stood on the summit of Cemetery Hill with Union artillery in their hands.

On the slope below, Colonel Isaac Avery was shot through the neck. He knew he was dying. Unable to speak, he found a pencil and a scrap of paper and wrote with a shaking hand: 'Tell my father I died with my face to the enemy.'

Then he wrote his father's name, and died.

On the summit, Carroll's Union brigade counterattacked. Without Confederate infantry support coming behind them, Hays and the survivors of Avery's command could not hold. They came back down the hill in the darkness, back through the town, back to their starting line.

They had touched the crest. They had held the guns. They had come closer to breaking the Union center than any Confederate force at Gettysburg.

But it was not enough.

stories.title: Mudge and the Charge at Culp's Hill
stories.summary: Lieutenant Colonel Charles Mudge was ordered to lead his 2nd Massachusetts Infantry in a charge across open ground toward Confederate positions at Culp's Hill. He protested the order. When told it was confirmed, he said: 'It is murder but it is the order.' He led the charge and was killed instantly. The regiment suffered 43% casualties in minutes.
stories.script:
The order came down at approximately 7:30 in the morning of July 3.

Colonize Silas Colgrove had received instructions to clear Confederate infantry from their position at the base of Culp's Hill. The 2nd Massachusetts and the 27th Indiana were to charge across an open meadow -- perhaps 200 yards of ground fully exposed to Confederate fire from the woods beyond.

Lieutenant Colonel Charles Mudge commanded the 2nd Massachusetts. He read the order and then read it again.

He sent an aide back to Colgrove. Was the order correct? Had there been a mistake?

The aide came back. The order was confirmed.

Mudge looked at the meadow. He looked at his regiment -- 316 men who had served through two years of war, who had marched from Maryland to Pennsylvania, who trusted him.

He turned to his officers.

'It is murder,' he said. 'But it is the order.'

He drew his saber and led the 2nd Massachusetts across the meadow at the double-quick.

The Confederate fire from the woods was immediate and accurate. Men fell as they ran. Mudge was hit almost at once -- shot through the throat, killed instantly, falling in the open ground he had called murder to cross.

The regiment reached the Confederate position, could not hold it, and withdrew. In the few minutes of the charge and its aftermath, 136 of 316 men were casualties -- 43 percent.

The 27th Indiana charged alongside them. It did not go better.

Colgrove's charge is still debated. Some accounts suggest the order was given in confusion, that it was never meant to be a frontal assault across open ground. Whatever the intent, the result was exactly what Mudge had predicted.

His last words -- 'It is murder but it is the order' -- are among the most quoted of the battle.

stories.title: The Cannonade
stories.summary: At approximately 1:00pm on July 3, two Confederate signal guns fired in sequence and 170 guns erupted along Seminary Ridge -- the largest artillery bombardment ever seen on the North American continent. The sound was heard in Philadelphia, 140 miles away. Alexander's guns fired for nearly two hours before Pickett stepped off.
stories.script:
At one o'clock in the afternoon, two signal guns fired from Seminary Ridge.

Then 170 guns fired at once.

The sound was heard in Pittsburgh. Some accounts place it as far as Philadelphia -- 140 miles to the east. The smoke rising from Seminary Ridge was visible for twenty miles. Every gun in Alexander's command, every gun in the Third Corps artillery, every piece that could bear on Cemetery Ridge fired simultaneously and continued firing.

Alexander had positioned his guns with extraordinary care. They stretched for nearly two miles along Seminary Ridge, wheel to wheel in places, the barrels elevated slightly to reach the distant blue line on Cemetery Ridge. The Washington Artillery of New Orleans -- the most famous artillery unit in the Confederate army -- was in the line. Pegram's battalion fired from the northern end. Cabell's and Henry's battalions fired from the south.

On Cemetery Ridge, the Union infantry pressed themselves flat behind the stone walls and into the shallow hollows and swales of the ground. The Confederate fire was intense but, as Hunt had feared, much of it was overshooting -- landing behind the ridge near the Taneytown Road, destroying caissons and limbers, killing horses and headquarters staff, nearly hitting Meade himself.

Hunt watched the fire carefully. He began deliberately silencing the Union guns -- battery by battery, pulling them back or having them cease fire. He was conserving ammunition for what he knew was coming. Hancock, riding the line and watching his infantry press closer to the ground, overruled him on some batteries: keep firing, he said. The men need to see their guns fighting.

For nearly two hours the ground shook.

Then Alexander sent his first message to Pickett.

And then the guns fell silent, and across the open fields of Pennsylvania, 12,500 men in gray and butternut stepped out of the tree line and began to walk east.

stories.title: Alexander's Two Messages
stories.summary: As the Confederate cannonade approached its end, Colonel Edward Porter Alexander sent two messages to General Pickett that define the moment when the charge became inevitable. The first urged haste -- ammunition was nearly gone. The second, the most ominous, told Pickett that Alexander himself would not advise making the charge -- but that the order had been given and the troops were already moving.
stories.script:
Colonel Edward Porter Alexander was twenty-eight years old, the chief of artillery for Longstreet's corps, and the man responsible for directing the greatest artillery bombardment in the history of the Western Hemisphere.

For two hours, 170 Confederate guns had been firing at Cemetery Ridge. The Union guns had fallen mostly silent. To Alexander, watching from Seminary Ridge through the smoke and dust, it looked like the cannonade might have worked. The ridge appeared quieter.

But Alexander was running out of ammunition. The Confederate army had no ammunition reserve close enough to replenish the batteries before the infantry assault. When the guns stopped firing, there would be nothing left for close support.

He wrote his first message to Pickett:

'General: If you are to advance at all, you must come at once or I cannot give you proper support, but the enemy's fire has not slackened materially and at least eighteen guns are still firing from the Cemetery itself.'

Pickett showed the message to Longstreet. Longstreet, who had spent two days arguing against this assault, could not speak. He bowed his head.

Alexander watched the ridge. The Union guns were still silent. He wrote a second message:

'For God's sake come quick. The eighteen guns have gone. Come quick or my ammunition won't let me support you properly.'

Pickett came to Longstreet. 'General, shall I advance?'

Longstreet turned away. He could not order it. He bowed his head again.

Pickett understood. He rode to his division.

Alexander never forgot what he had done. In his memoir, written decades later, he wrote that when he sent that first message he had not understood what he was setting in motion -- that he was, in effect, writing the death warrant for thousands of men. If he had known the ammunition supply was nearly gone, he wrote, he would have urged Longstreet to stop the assault entirely.

'I would not make the charge now,' he had written in a later message. 'But the order has been given and the troops are already moving.'

They were.

stories.title: Armistead at The Angle
stories.summary: Brigadier General Lewis Armistead placed his hat on his sword as a guide and led his brigade over the stone wall at The Angle -- the deepest Confederate penetration of the battle. He was shot down moments later, falling among Union troops beyond the wall. His old friend Winfield Hancock was wounded simultaneously on the other side of the ridge. Both men lay bleeding at the High Water Mark of the Confederacy.
stories.script:
Lewis Armistead and Winfield Hancock had been friends since before the war -- close friends, the kind of friends that the old army made of men who served together in remote posts for years. When Virginia seceded, Armistead had gone south. On the night before he left California, at a farewell party, he had placed his hands on Hancock's shoulders and wept. 'Hancock, goodbye,' he said. 'You can never know what this has cost me.'

That was two years before Gettysburg.

Now Armistead led what remained of his Virginia brigade across the open ground toward Cemetery Ridge. The cannonade had cleared some of the Union guns. There was a gap -- a real gap -- in the line ahead, near a low stone wall and a copse of trees.

Armistead placed his black felt hat on the tip of his sword, raising it above his head as a guide for his men in the smoke and confusion. He walked forward -- not ran, walked, with a deliberate stride. Ahead was the wall.

He stepped over the wall. Behind him, perhaps 150 men followed.

Lieutenant Alonzo Cushing had been serving his last two guns at that wall all afternoon, wounded twice already, holding the battery together through sheer will. When Armistead's men came over the wall, Cushing was at his gun. He was shot through the mouth and killed.

Armistead reached out and touched one of Cushing's guns. A moment later he was shot -- the exact details are disputed, but he fell within the Union lines, beyond the wall.

He was carried to the Union rear. As he lay dying, he asked for Hancock to be brought to him. He did not know that Hancock, on the other side of the ridge, had been wounded almost simultaneously -- a nail and saddle pommel fragment driven deep into his thigh.

Both men lay bleeding. The Confederacy had reached its High Water Mark.

Armistead died two days later. He never saw Hancock again.

The stone wall at The Angle, the copse of trees behind it, and the ground where Armistead fell are preserved today exactly as they were on the afternoon of July 3, 1863. A monument marks the spot where he went down.

stories.title: Cushing's Battery
stories.summary: Lieutenant Alonzo Cushing served his last two guns at The Angle through the Confederate cannonade and Pickett's assault, twice wounded but refusing to leave. He was killed while firing at Armistead's men crossing the wall -- shot through the mouth. He received the Medal of Honor in 2014, 151 years after his death -- the longest gap between action and award in the history of the decoration.
stories.script:
Alonzo Cushing was twenty-two years old.

He had graduated from West Point in 1861 and commanded Battery A, 4th US Artillery -- six three-inch rifles positioned directly behind the stone wall at The Angle, at the exact focal point of the Confederate assault.

The cannonade had been brutal for his battery. Horses killed. Men down. Two of his six guns disabled. By the time Pickett's infantry appeared at the tree line, Cushing had four guns serviceable and was wounded himself -- a fragment through the shoulder.

As the Confederate line crossed the Emmitsburg Road and came on, Cushing took another hit. The wound was grave -- a shell fragment through the groin. His sergeant, Frederick Fuger, urged him to go to the rear.

Cushing refused. He had two guns left. He would serve them himself.

With Fuger's help, he moved his last two guns to the wall itself -- the stone wall at The Angle -- and loaded them with double canister. As Armistead's men climbed over the wall on his left, as the Union line bent and buckled around him, Cushing fired one last round of canister into the Confederate infantry at a range of perhaps twenty yards.

He was shot through the mouth.

Fuger assumed command of what remained of the battery. The Angle held.

Cushing's family petitioned for a Medal of Honor for the next century and a half. The Army reviewed the case repeatedly. Bureaucratic obstacles -- the statute of limitations, administrative requirements -- delayed the award for generations.

On November 6, 2014, President Obama presented the Medal of Honor to a descendant of Cushing's family at a White House ceremony. Alonzo Cushing received the nation's highest military honor 151 years after he died earning it -- the longest gap between action and award in the history of the decoration.

He was twenty-two years old.

stories.title: Pickett's Return
stories.summary: After the repulse of Pickett's Charge, Lee rode forward to meet his broken men and told them repeatedly: 'It is all my fault.' General Pickett, asked by Lee to reform his division for defense, replied: 'General Lee, I have no division.' Pickett never forgave Lee for ordering the charge and never recovered from the loss of his men.
stories.script:
George Pickett sat on his horse and watched his division come back.

They came in clusters and straggles, the survivors of a mile-wide charge across open ground under artillery and musketry. Some walked steadily. Some stumbled. Some were helping others walk. All of them had the look of men who had been through something that no words could explain.

Of the three brigades Pickett had sent forward -- Garnett, Kemper, Armistead -- Garnett was dead, Kemper was critically wounded and briefly a prisoner, Armistead was dying beyond the stone wall he had crossed. The division had suffered nearly 2,700 casualties from 5,500 engaged. Forty-nine percent.

Lee rode forward to meet them.

He rode along the broken line, and he said to them, over and over, the same thing: 'It is all my fault. It is I who have lost this fight, and you must help me out of it the best you can.'

Pickett came to Lee. Lee told him to reform his division -- there might be a Union counterattack coming.

Pickett looked at Lee. 'General Lee,' he said, 'I have no division.'

Lee never acknowledged, officially or privately, that ordering the charge had been a mistake. He praised the courage of his men and said that more support should have been provided. In his official report he blamed himself in the most general terms.

Pickett blamed Lee specifically. For the rest of his life he told anyone who would listen that Lee had destroyed his division. When someone praised Lee in Pickett's presence years after the war, Pickett said quietly: 'That man destroyed my division.'

He said it with the measured tone of a man who had been carrying the weight of it for decades.

stories.title: Lee Meets His Men
stories.place: Open fields west of Cemetery Ridge
stories.summary: As the survivors of Pickett's Charge streamed back toward Seminary Ridge, Robert E. Lee rode out to meet them personally, telling them repeatedly: 'It is all my fault.' Imboden, who was with Lee that evening, described him pacing back and forth saying 'Too bad. Too bad. Oh, too bad.' It was the closest Lee ever came to public acknowledgment of error.
stories.script:
General John Imboden had been ordered to prepare for the retreat. He was waiting near Lee's headquarters when the survivors of Pickett's Charge began coming back across the fields.

Lee rode out to meet them.

He rode slowly along the broken line of men, and Imboden watched from nearby. What he saw, he wrote later, he never forgot.

Lee rode among his men and said to them, over and over: 'All this has been my fault -- it is I who have lost this fight, and you must help me out of it the best you can.' Some of the men reached up and touched his boots as he passed. Some wept.

When Pickett came to him, Lee said: 'Come, General Pickett. This has been my fight, and upon my shoulders rests the blame.'

That night, Lee found Imboden waiting for him.

'General,' Imboden said, 'this has been a hard day on you.'

Lee said nothing at first. He sat on his horse in the darkness. Then he began to talk, and Imboden wrote down what he said as carefully as he could remember:

'I never saw troops behave more magnificently than Pickett's division of Virginians did today in that grand charge upon the enemy. And if they had been supported as they were to have been -- but for some reason not yet fully explained -- the charge would have been gloriously successful.'

Then Lee fell silent again. He seemed to be speaking almost to himself.

'Too bad. Too bad. Oh, too bad.'

Imboden heard him say it over and over as they rode back toward headquarters.

Lee never said it quite so plainly again.

stories.title: Custer at East Cavalry Field
stories.summary: Three miles east of Gettysburg, while Pickett's infantry was being repulsed at The Angle, Stuart's cavalry attempted to sweep around the Union rear. The 23-year-old General George Armstrong Custer personally led the Michigan Brigade in a mounted charge that stopped Stuart cold. 'Come on, you Wolverines!' he shouted -- and they came.
stories.script:
George Armstrong Custer was twenty-three years old and had been a brigadier general for exactly eight days.

He had earned the promotion through a combination of extraordinary courage and extraordinary luck -- the kind of officer who seemed to attract bullets that always missed.
