He wore a custom uniform of black velvet with gold trim that made him conspicuous on any battlefield. He wore his hair in long golden ringlets. He was, in the Army of the Potomac, impossible to ignore.

On the afternoon of July 3, while Pickett's infantry was crossing the open fields toward Cemetery Ridge, Stuart's cavalry moved east of Gettysburg to sweep around the Union rear. If Stuart could strike the Union rear simultaneously with the infantry assault on the front, the Army of the Potomac might be destroyed.

Gregg's cavalry division blocked the road. Custer's Michigan Brigade -- 1,900 troopers on fresh horses -- was the striking force.

Stuart advanced. Hampton's South Carolinians and Fitz Lee's Virginians moved forward in what Confederate veterans later described as a magnificent charge -- thousands of horsemen covering the ground in a sweeping wall of cavalry.

Custer rode to the front of his brigade. He turned to his Wolverines.

'Come on, you Wolverines!'

He spurred his horse directly at the Confederate advance. The Michigan Brigade came with him.

The two lines met at a full gallop in the largest cavalry engagement of the Gettysburg campaign. Men sabre'd each other at close range, horses went down, the lines interpenetrated and dissolved into a melee of individual combats across a half-mile front. Hampton was wounded -- a sabre cut to the head.

When it was over, Stuart's cavalry fell back. The Union rear was secure.

On Cemetery Ridge, the last of Pickett's men were streaming back from The Angle.

Custer had done his part.

stories.title: Farnsworth's Charge
stories.summary: General Elon Farnsworth had been a general for eight days when Kilpatrick ordered him to charge Confederate infantry over rocky terrain south of the battlefield. Farnsworth protested that the charge was suicidal. Kilpatrick insisted. Farnsworth led the charge and was killed. He had been a general for exactly four days when he died.
stories.script:
Elon Farnsworth had been a general for eight days.

He had the promotion because he was a good cavalry officer and because his uncle was an influential congressman and because Pleasonton was promoting young men he trusted. Eight days -- long enough to receive the commission, pin on the stars, and die.

Kilpatrick ordered him to charge.

Farnsworth looked at the ground ahead. It was a nightmare of boulders and fencing and rocky terrain, defended by Law's Confederate infantry and the dismounted men of Robertson's Texas Brigade. Cavalry -- even the best cavalry -- could not charge formed infantry over ground like that.

He said so.

Kilpatrick, in the accounts that survive, challenged his courage. The exact words are disputed, but the meaning was clear: charge, or be thought a coward.

Farnsworth's face went white. Then he said something that the men nearby remembered for the rest of their lives -- an expression of outrage, of contempt, and of acceptance, all in one breath. He would lead the charge himself.

'If you order the charge, I will lead it,' he said. 'But if we go in there it will be a charge of death.'

Kilpatrick ordered the charge.

Farnsworth rode to the front of his brigade and led them forward into the rocks and the Confederate fire.

He was shot five times. He fell among the boulders south of Big Round Top, a general for four days.

The charge accomplished nothing. No Confederate position was taken, no Union position was relieved. The men who survived came back to their starting line having given nothing and gained nothing.

Kilpatrick's decision was condemned then and has been condemned since. He spent the rest of his life defending it.

stories.title: The High Water Mark
stories.summary: The Battle of Gettysburg ended on July 3, 1863 with approximately 51,000 casualties across three days -- the bloodiest battle ever fought on American soil. The spot where Armistead fell at The Angle is marked today as the High Water Mark of the Confederacy. The Army of Northern Virginia would never again invade the North.
stories.script:
The battle was over.

From the first shot on Knoxlyn Ridge on the morning of July 1 to the last cavalry action east of town on the afternoon of July 3, the Battle of Gettysburg had consumed three days and approximately 51,000 men. Seven thousand were dead. The rest were wounded or missing. The fields and orchards and woodlots of Adams County, Pennsylvania -- farmland, ordinary farmland -- were covered with the wreckage of two armies.

On July 4, while the town of Gettysburg tried to count its dead, the news arrived from the west: Vicksburg had fallen. Grant had split the Confederacy. Two disasters in two days.

Lee began his retreat on July 4 in a driving rainstorm. Imboden's wagon train -- seventeen miles of it, filled with wounded men who screamed with every jolt of the road -- moved south and west toward Virginia. The army followed, battered, depleted, but intact. Meade chose not to pursue aggressively. The opportunity to destroy Lee's army, if it existed, was not taken.

The Confederacy would fight on for nearly two more years. There would be Cold Harbor and the Wilderness and Petersburg and the Shenandoah and Appomattox. But the moment when Confederate victory was possible -- the moment when a successful invasion of the North might have forced a negotiated peace -- had passed on the afternoon of July 3 at a stone wall in Pennsylvania.

The copse of trees still stands. The stone wall has been rebuilt where it was torn apart in the fighting. A bronze marker -- placed by veterans, not the government -- stands near the spot where Armistead fell.

It reads: 'The High Water Mark of the Rebellion.'

The ground is quiet now. The fields are green in summer, brown in fall, white in winter. The monuments stand in long rows along Seminary Ridge and Cemetery Ridge and the slopes of Culp's Hill and Little Round Top. There are 1,328 of them -- more monuments per square mile than anywhere else on earth.

In July, when the heat is heavy and the air still, you can stand at The Angle and look west across the open fields and understand exactly what happened here, and why it mattered, and what it cost.

tour.title: McPherson Ridge
tour.subtitle: The Battle Begins — July 1, 7:30 AM
tour.narrative:
On the morning of July 1, 1863, Union cavalry under Brigadier General John Buford deployed along McPherson's Ridge west of Gettysburg. Buford recognized the strategic importance of the high ground and determined to hold it until infantry arrived.

When Heth's Confederate division advanced down the Chambersburg Pike, Buford's dismounted troopers fought a delaying action from behind fence rails and earthworks. Their stand bought precious time for Reynolds' I Corps to arrive.

General John Reynolds, one of the most respected officers in the Army of the Potomac, rode forward to direct the Iron Brigade into Herbst Woods. Minutes later, he was killed by a Confederate sharpshooter — one of the highest-ranking Union officers to die in the battle.

tour.title: Oak Ridge
tour.subtitle: The Union Right Flank — July 1, 10:00 AM
tour.narrative:
As the morning of July 1 progressed, Confederate forces under Rodes arrived on Oak Ridge north of the town, threatening the Union right flank. The XI Corps under Howard deployed north of Gettysburg to meet this threat.

Iverson's North Carolina brigade advanced without skirmishers into a deadly ambush. Paul's Union brigade, concealed behind a stone wall, delivered a devastating volley. Nearly 500 Confederates surrendered in the wheat field — the largest single mass surrender of the battle.

Daniel's brigade and Ramseur's brigade pressed the Union line relentlessly. By early afternoon the Union position north of town was becoming untenable.

tour.title: Barlow's Knoll
tour.subtitle: XI Corps Exposed — July 1, 2:30 PM
tour.narrative:
Brigadier General Francis Barlow advanced his division of the XI Corps to a slight rise north of Gettysburg — soon to bear his name. The move exposed both flanks and invited envelopment.

Early's division, arriving from the northeast on the Harrisburg Road, struck the exposed position from three sides simultaneously. Gordon's Georgia brigade swept forward with devastating effect.

Barlow was shot from his horse and left for dead on the field. Confederate General Gordon, finding him wounded, stopped to give him water and had him moved to safety. The two men would become friends after the war, debating for decades whether this encounter actually occurred.

tour.title: Seminary Ridge
tour.subtitle: The Union Retreat — July 1, 4:00 PM
tour.narrative:
By mid-afternoon on July 1, the Union position north and west of Gettysburg had become untenable. The XI Corps was streaming back through the town in disorder, and the I Corps' right flank was exposed.

The survivors rallied on Cemetery Hill south of town, where Howard had wisely positioned a reserve. The high ground — Cemetery Hill, Culp's Hill, and the long spine of Cemetery Ridge — would become the Union fishhook line that determined the battle's outcome.

General Hancock arrived by order of Meade to take command and restore order. His presence steadied the shaken troops. "I think this the strongest position by nature upon which to fight a battle that I ever saw," he reported to Meade.

tour.title: Little Round Top
tour.subtitle: The Race for the Summit — July 2, 4:00 PM
tour.narrative:
On the afternoon of July 2, Confederate forces under Hood's division discovered that Little Round Top — the rocky height anchoring the left of the Union line — was unoccupied. Law's Alabama brigade raced for the summit.

At almost the same moment, Meade's chief engineer spotted the danger and rushed Vincent's V Corps brigade to the hill. They arrived with minutes to spare.

The 20th Maine under Colonel Joshua Lawrence Chamberlain held the extreme left of the entire Union army. When the regiment's ammunition ran low after multiple Confederate assaults, Chamberlain ordered a bayonet charge downhill. The unexpected assault routed the exhausted 15th Alabama and secured the position.

tour.title: Devil's Den
tour.subtitle: The Triangular Field — July 2, 4:30 PM
tour.narrative:
Below Little Round Top, the massive boulders of Devil's Den provided a natural fortress. Hood's Texas Brigade fought its way through the rocky terrain, driving Ward's Union brigade from the position.

Confederate sharpshooters occupied the crevices among the boulders and fired on Little Round Top throughout the afternoon. The famous photograph of a Confederate sharpshooter dead among the rocks was later revealed to have been staged by photographer Alexander Gardner.

The fighting in the triangular field between Devil's Den and the Wheatfield was some of the most confused and brutal of the entire battle.

tour.title: The Wheatfield
tour.subtitle: Six Times Contested — July 2, 5:00 PM
tour.narrative:
The 26-acre Wheatfield of farmer George Rose became one of the bloodiest patches of ground in American military history on the afternoon of July 2. The field changed hands at least six times during three hours of fighting.

Kershaw's South Carolina brigade attacked through Rose's Woods. de Trobriand's brigade and then Sweitzer's formed successive defensive lines. Caldwell's entire II Corps division — all four brigades under Cross, Kelly, Zook, and Brooke — countercharged through the field.

Brigadier General Samuel Zook was mortally wounded leading his brigade into the fight. Colonel Patrick Kelly's Irish Brigade advanced with green sprigs of boxwood in their caps, a Celtic tradition before battle. By nightfall, approximately 4,000 men lay killed or wounded in this single field.

tour.title: Peach Orchard
tour.subtitle: Sickles' Salient Falls — July 2, 6:00 PM
tour.narrative:
General Daniel Sickles, the controversial III Corps commander, advanced his corps a mile forward from the assigned position on Cemetery Ridge to the higher ground around the Peach Orchard. The move created a vulnerable salient with exposed flanks on both sides.

Barksdale's Mississippi brigade — 1,400 men — charged the Peach Orchard with Barksdale riding at their front. The assault swept through the orchard and shattered the III Corps.

Sickles himself was struck by a cannonball that mangled his leg. He was carried from the field smoking a cigar, reportedly to reassure his men. His leg was amputated; he later donated it to the Army Medical Museum, where he visited it annually for the rest of his life.

tour.title: Cemetery Hill
tour.subtitle: The Tigers Assault the Guns — July 2, 8:00 PM
tour.narrative:
As darkness fell on July 2, Hays' Louisiana Tigers and Avery's North Carolina brigade launched a twilight assault on Cemetery Hill. The attackers swept up the slope and overran Wiedrich's and Ricketts' batteries.

For ten desperate minutes, Confederate soldiers fought among the Union cannon with rammers, handspikes, and bare hands. It was the closest any Confederate force came to capturing Cemetery Hill during the entire battle.

Brigadier General Isaac Avery was mortally wounded during the advance. As he lay dying, he scrawled a final message on a scrap of paper using his own blood: "Tell my father I died with my face to the enemy." Carroll's II Corps brigade countercharged and drove the Confederates back down the hill.

tour.title: Culp's Hill
tour.subtitle: The Overnight Fight — July 2-3
tour.narrative:
While the fighting raged on the Union left on July 2, Johnson's Confederate division attacked the right flank at Culp's Hill. Greene's New York brigade — only 1,400 men — held a mile of trenches against nearly 4,700 attackers through the night.

Greene's men benefited from the solid earthworks they had constructed, firing from protected positions while Confederate attackers struggled uphill through dense woods in darkness. The fight continued sporadically through the night.

At dawn on July 3, the XII Corps returned from Cemetery Ridge and launched a series of assaults to recover the lost trenches. The fighting continued for seven hours — the longest sustained engagement of the three-day battle.

tour.title: Cemetery Ridge
tour.subtitle: Wright's Breakthrough — July 2, 7:30 PM
tour.narrative:
In the fading light of July 2, Ambrose Wright's Georgia brigade achieved what no other Confederate force managed that day: they crested Cemetery Ridge and briefly reached the Baltimore Pike.

"We were on the crest," Wright later wrote. "We had pierced the enemy's lines." But Posey's and Mahone's brigades, which were supposed to support Wright's flanks, failed to advance. Hit from three sides, Wright's unsupported men were driven back.

Hancock rushed every available man to seal the breach. The crisis passed — but it showed Lee that the Union center could be broken. The observation would inform his decision to order Pickett's Charge the following day.

tour.title: The Angle
tour.subtitle: The High-Water Mark — July 3, 3:00 PM
tour.narrative:
At 3:00 PM on July 3, the survivors of the mile-long advance reached the stone wall at The Angle. Armistead, with his hat raised on his sword so men could see him through the smoke, called out: "Come on boys, give them the cold steel!"

Armistead led approximately 150 men over the wall and reached Cushing's guns. Artillery Lieutenant Alonzo Cushing had remained at his battery despite being wounded twice, holding his intestines with one hand while commanding with the other. He was shot through the head at the moment of Armistead's breakthrough.

Armistead fell wounded at the guns. Told that his old friend Hancock was also wounded nearby, he asked that his watch and personal effects be delivered to Hancock with his regrets. Armistead died two days later.

tour.title: East Cavalry Field
tour.subtitle: Stuart vs. Custer — July 3, 3:00 PM
tour.narrative:
While Pickett's Charge unfolded a mile to the west, JEB Stuart's cavalry attempted to reach the Baltimore Pike and strike Meade's rear. Four Confederate brigades — Hampton, Fitz Lee, Chambliss, and Jenkins — advanced toward the Union rear.

Gregg's Union cavalry division, reinforced by Custer's Michigan brigade, blocked the advance. The 23-year-old George Armstrong Custer charged Hampton's brigade at full gallop with the 7th Michigan, shouting "Come on, you Wolverines!"

The collision of the two cavalry forces stopped Stuart cold. Hampton was wounded. By the time Pickett's Charge had failed, there was no longer any rear to strike. Stuart withdrew, and the East Cavalry Field action passed largely unnoticed amid the drama at The Angle.

tour.title: Pickett's Charge
tour.subtitle: The Mile-Wide Advance — July 3, 3:00 PM
tour.narrative:
At 1:07 PM on July 3, 1863, Confederate artillery opened the greatest bombardment in the history of the Western Hemisphere — 150 guns firing simultaneously at Cemetery Ridge. The cannonade lasted nearly two hours.

At approximately 3:00 PM, 12,500 Confederate soldiers stepped from the tree line on Seminary Ridge and began the mile-wide advance. Pickett's division, Pettigrew's division, and Trimble's two brigades crossed the open ground under devastating artillery and musket fire.

The charge reached The Angle but was repulsed at enormous cost. Confederate casualties were approximately 50% — over 6,000 men killed, wounded, or captured. Lee rode among the survivors saying "It is all my fault." The charge marked the beginning of the end of Confederate offensive capacity.

tour.title: The High Water Mark
tour.subtitle: The Copse of Trees — July 3
tour.narrative:
A small copse of trees on Cemetery Ridge served as the visual aiming point for Pickett's Charge and has since become known as the High Water Mark of the Confederacy — the point of maximum Confederate penetration into the Union line.

The monument at the High Water Mark was dedicated in 1892. The Battlefield Memorial Association, which later became part of the NPS, was established partly to preserve this ground.

General Lewis Armistead, who died after being wounded at the guns, is remembered by a marker near the copse of trees. His friendship with Union General Winfield Hancock — wounded the same afternoon — became one of the war's most poignant symbols of a nation divided against itself.

tour.title: Confederate Avenue
tour.subtitle: The Retreat — July 4-5, 1863
tour.narrative:
On the night of July 4-5, 1863, the Army of Northern Virginia began its retreat toward Virginia. A wagon train of wounded men, 17 miles long, moved through driving rain toward the Potomac crossing at Williamsport.

Meade chose not to pursue aggressively. President Lincoln was devastated by the failure to destroy Lee's army before it could cross the Potomac. "We had them within our grasp," Lincoln wrote. "We had only to stretch forth our hands and they were ours."

Lee's army crossed the swollen Potomac on July 14, escaping to Virginia. The Gettysburg campaign was over. Confederate casualties totaled approximately 28,000; Union casualties approximately 23,000. The battle proved to be the turning point of the war in the East.
